Tonight: AI in the physical world — and how we try to guarantee safety.

01An old story

Therac‑25, 1985–87: dangers with new technologies

A radiation‑therapy machine. Six massive overdoses in two years, across the US and Canada. Three patients died of the overdose.

The design

Earlier models had hardware interlocks — physical switches that made dangerous behaviors impossible. Software checks were substituted for many traditional hardware interlocks.

The bug

A race condition: an operator who edited the prescription too quickly could trigger the raw beam to fire without shielding.

The detail that should stop us

The Therac‑20 contained the same software error but its hardware caught what the software missed.

Three years of investigation: “system testing alone is not adequate.”

01An old story

Intel Pentium, 1994: an expensive typo

Cost of the recall
$0

Intel's answer ever since:
mathematically prove the arithmetic,
don't just test it.

01An old story

Ariane 5, 1996: one number too big for its box

The bug

A 64‑bit decimal was forced into a 16‑bit integer slot and overflowed, in code that serves no purpose after lift‑off, kept from Ariane 4 “for commonality”.

The failure

Two inertial reference computers ran identical software — so both halted, 0.05 s apart. The autopilot then steered on their error message as if it were flight data.

The code had flown for years — on Ariane 4, a slower rocket. “Correct” is always relative to a specification — change the rocket and the guarantee changes too.

01An old story

Mars Climate Orbiter, 1999: pounds versus newtons

The bug

The ground software reported thruster impulses in pound‑force seconds; the interface specification said newton seconds.

The failure

Nine months of navigation quietly absorbed the 4.45× error. The $125 M orbiter’s first pass came in at an estimated 57 km — below the ≈80 km survival line.

The right unit was written down. A specification only protects you if something checks it.

03Why we’re turning to AI

AI capabilities have jumped in the last 10 years

To 2011 — hand‑designed features

A person decided in advance what to measure — edges at particular angles, corners, patches of texture — and wrote it down as code. The computer only scored features a human had chosen.

2012 onward — learned features

Nobody writes the features down. The network starts from random numbers, sees 1.2 M labelled photographs, and every mistake nudges each number a little. Useful features appear on their own.

Where no first‑principles model exists, fitting to data beats writing rules. Retinal scans, skin lesions, speech, driving: the same curve. Caveat: 3.6% is an average over one fixed test set.

03Why we’re turning to AI

Learned controllers are beating classical control

🏁
Drone racing — Swift Kaufmann et al., Nature 2023

Beat three champion pilots — two of them world champions — 15 races to 10.

☀️
Fusion plasma — TCV tokamak Degrave et al., Nature 2022

One reinforcement‑learned policy replaced a bank of separate PID loops.

🐕
Legged robots — ANYmal Lee 2020 · Miki 2022, Sci. Robotics

Trained in simulation; crossed mud and rubble where the model‑based controller fell.

🌦️
Weather — GraphCast Lam et al., Science 2023

A 36.7 M‑parameter graph neural network beat ECMWF’s operational physics model.

Classical control is still vital but data can help us close gaps to real behavior.

03Why we’re turning to AI

Why did AI suddenly get so good?

1 · Labels were the bottleneck

ImageNet: 1.2 M photographs, each labelled by a person.

2 · Self‑supervised learning (GPT, 2018)

Objective: predict the next token — the data labels itself, so the training set can be the whole internet.

3 · Transformer (2017) + scaling laws (2020)

An architecture that introduces context — and more data and compute keep helping, predictably.

“General methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective, and by a large margin.”
— Richard Sutton, The Bitter Lesson, 2019
03Why we’re turning to AI

The second recent jump in capability — an example

Previously task specific tools (gray)

Trained on 960 h of clean audiobooks. Superb there — brittle everywhere else.

Whisper (OpenAI, 2022)

Trained on 680,000 hours of everyday audio from the web — 700× more, most of it noisy.

On speech neither had seen — and it still ties the specialist on the specialist’s own benchmark.

The breakthrough: breadth also appears to bring robustness.

04The problem

Images are points; perturbations lie in an ε‑ball

A photo is a vector of pixel values — a point in a million‑dimensional input space.

All imperceptible perturbations of the photo form an ε‑ball of radius ε around that point.

An adversarial perturbation slides the point in the ε‑ball — across the network’s decision boundary.

04The problem

Is there any point in the ε‑ball
that flips the label?

The ε‑ball contains infinitely many images.
No amount of testing can try them all.

“Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence!”
— Edsger Dijkstra, 1970
04The problem

Adversarial examples: imperceptible perturbations

Audio adversarial examples: a clip that sounds like ordinary talk transcribes as “okay google, browse to evil.com” — any audio, any target phrase.

Physical‑world adversarial example: a few stickers, and a stop sign is classified as “Speed limit 45.”

LLM jailbreaks are adversarial examples too: one optimised suffix of gibberish tokens, and an aligned chatbot writes the malicious code it just refused to write.

04The problem

The Turing Award keeps going to formal methods

The ACM A.M. Turing Award — “the Nobel Prize in Computing” — has 81 laureates. Twelve of them laid the foundations of formal methods: the logics, automata and algorithms for proving that programs do what they should.

Reasoning about programs
Automata · semantics · proof assistants
Complexity
Temporal logic · model checking
Concurrency

06From images to machines

One method, many specifications

Robustness

Every image in the ε‑ball around this photo gets the same label — noise, dirt, glare and all.

Fairness

Two applicants who differ only in a protected attribute must get the same decision — provably.

Reachability

Where can the closed‑loop system — network and physics — be, one second from now?

The ε‑ball of “nearby images” becomes a set of people, scripts of code , or of aircraft states. The maths doesn’t mind.

05Opening the box

A neural network: affine layers + ReLU activations

1 · Affine layer — multiply & add

Wx + b — like 3×flour + 2×sugar. Well‑behaved, fully predictable.

2 · ReLU — max(0, x)

The only non‑linearity. All the intelligence — and all the trouble — lives here.

05Opening the box

Affine layers propagate the whole set at once

So instead of testing images one at a time, we propagate the entire infinite ε‑ball through the layer in one step.

05Opening the box

ReLU is not linear — it is piecewise linear

Approach 1 — exact: split the set and each half meets an affine map again — handled exactly, no approximation anywhere. The price: one set becomes two.

05Opening the box

Every straddled ReLU doubles the sets

Inside a real network, every ReLU the set straddles forces the split — one set becomes two.

Each set meets more ReLUs in the next layer.
Two becomes four. Four becomes eight…

State‑space explosion

Just 50 straddled ReLUs → 2⁵⁰ ≈ 1,000,000,000,000,000 activation patterns. More than we can store.

05A $1,000,000 aside

Verifying a ReLU network is NP‑complete

In 2017, researchers proved ReLU network verification is NP‑complete — it joins the class of problems computer science believes admit no polynomial‑time algorithm.

Whether that class truly has no polynomial‑time algorithm is the P vs NP problem — one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems. Solve it: $1,000,000.

Only one of the seven has ever fallen — though this month an AI‑generated proof of Navier–Stokes is under review. For P vs NP, ~9 in 10 experts bet P ≠ NP. So we don’t wait for a polynomial‑time algorithm — we over‑approximate.

05Opening the box

Approach 2 — over‑approximation

05Opening the box

Abstract domains: box, zonotope, polyhedron

05Opening the box

Two methods: both sound, only one complete

Exact — sound & complete
✅ “Safe” means verified safe
❌ “Unsafe” comes with a real counterexample
…but the state space explodes. Only small networks finish.
Over‑approximate — sound
✅ “Safe” still means verified safe — it contains the true reachable set
⚠️ “Unsafe” might be spurious — a real counterexample, or just looseness?
…but it scales to real networks, fast.

In practice, a hybrid: over‑approximate first; case‑split only where “unsafe” appears.

06From images to machines

Zoom out: where formal methods already run

☁️
Amazon’s cloud database

Formal verification caught a data‑loss bug that needed a 35‑step chain of events to appear. No test plan on Earth finds that.

✈️
Airbus fly‑by‑wire

Formal verification proves the flight code is free of runtime errors — for every input, on every flight.

🔒
seL4 — an operating‑system kernel

Ships with a machine‑checked proof that the code matches its formal specification, line by line.

🛠️
CompCert — a verified compiler

Bug‑hunters found hundreds of bugs in mainstream rivals — and none in its formally verified core.

Industry’s sentence is changing — from “we tested it extensively”
to “we proved it cannot do the bad thing.”

06From images to machines

Reachability: one reach tube, every possible future

06From images to machines

Formal specifications: what “behaves” means

Safety

the bad thing never happens

Reach‑avoid

reach the goal set, avoiding the unsafe set

Liveness

the good thing eventually happens

Resilience

after a disturbance, recover within k steps

Written in temporal logic — mathematics for sentences about time:
□ ¬crash  ·  ◇ goal  ·  dip → ◇≤k recover

06From images to machines

The safety certificate can itself be a network

A barrier certificate is a function B(x), non‑increasing along every trajectory — so its zero level set is never crossed.

1 · A network proposes the barrier

Learned from data — even when the system’s dynamics are unknown.

2 · A formal checker verifies it

Conditions hold? Keep it — the certificate. Violated? The counterexample goes back into training. Repeat.

The network is allowed to be creative, because it never gets the last word. The checker does.

09Where the field is heading

2024: the year the big prizes went to machine learning

Nobel Prize in Physics — Hopfield & Hinton

“for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks”. Hopfield network (1982): 30 nodes, 435 connections. Boltzmann machine (1985). Hinton also holds the 2018 Turing Award.

Nobel Prize in Chemistry — Baker · Hassabis & Jumper

Half “for computational protein design”; half “for protein structure prediction”. AlphaFold2: structures for nearly all ~200 million known proteins; at CASP14 (2020), median backbone error 0.96 Å against 2.8 Å.

AB
ACM Turing Award — Barto & Sutton

“for developing the conceptual and algorithmic foundations of reinforcement learning”. Temporal‑difference learning (Sutton, 1988); the textbook (1998). The paradigm behind the tokamak and ANYmal controllers of slide 16.

“…when we create digital beings that are more intelligent than ourselves. We have no idea whether we can stay in control.”
— Geoffrey Hinton, Nobel banquet speech, 10 December 2024
08What we can do

Answer 1 — probabilistic certificates

🎙️
Air‑traffic control, by radio

“Speedbird 245, descend flight level 80” — heard by a 1.5‑billion‑parameter speech model over a noisy VHF channel.

Sample channel noise 1,000 times

Independent draws of real VHF‑band noise. Count how often the meaning survives — which aircraft was addressed, which altitude was given.

The certificate 📜

“For the next, unheard burst of noise: under 5% probability the meaning changes — Clopper–Pearson, confidence 99.9999%.”

No exact verifier scales this far; sampling needs only forward passes.

08What we can do

Answer 2 — input‑agnostic certificates

Level 1 — per‑input (local) certificates
✗

each sign: 1,000 noise samples → its own local certificate

Level 2 — population certificate
📜 “At least 9 in 10 of the images this camera will ever meet are robust — confidence 99.9999%.”

The tested images become random samples themselves — a second scenario‑approach bound covers unseen inputs: images nobody has seen yet.

08What we can do

Answer 3 — runtime monitoring

A verified controller is flying — but its proof was made against a model of the world. On board, every split‑second, the monitor checks model against reality.

The moment they diverge — the world doing something the model never promised — a second controller steps in and corrects the course.

We flew it — a union of neural control barrier certificates, in our cluttered two‑room lab, through a 90 cm doorway. With the monitor: 0 of 4,810 states left the certified set. Without it: 177.
Fig. 3, work under review

09Where the field is heading

New architectures, new verification problems

Mixture of experts — sparse activation

A router wakes 2 of 8 experts per token — most of the network stays dark.

top‑k routing is a hard case split — the ReLU split of slide 28, over whole sub‑networks

Kolmogorov–Arnold networks — learnable edges

The learned pieces live on the edges, as splines — interpretable, ≈10× slower to train.

small symbolic pieces can be handed to an SMT solver: KAN barrier certificates (IJCAI 2025)

Graph neural networks — message passing

Each node listens to its neighbours — molecules, power grids, the weather model of slide 16.

unbounded graphs: reachability undecidable; bound the node degree and it becomes decidable (Sälzer & Lange, ICLR 2023)

Every new architecture re‑asks the question of slide 28: where do the case splits hide?

09Where the field is heading

Neuromorphic hardware: the brain runs on ≈20 W

Spiking, event‑driven chips

Energy spent only on events: TrueNorth classified video at 63 mW; Hala Point packs 1.15 B neurons — research prototypes.

The fine print

Intel’s own survey: ordinary feedforward networks see “modest if any benefit” — the gains need spikes used as spikes.

Why it matters

Data centres: ≈415 TWh in 2024, heading for ≈945 TWh by 2030, AI the main driver (IEA 2025).

robustness must cover spike timing too — today’s SNN verifiers are “barely scalable” (Seong et al., 2024)
